newsitem.title: GREECE: More unions join Greece's strike wave.
newsitem.headline: More unions join Greece's strike wave.

text.p: Greek high school teachers joined striking seamen in work stoppages on Monday and a nationwide general strike was scheduled for Thursday against the government's tough incomes and tax policies.

An eight-day strike by seamen, affecting all ships with Greek crews, has kept most vessels idle at ports. Minor clashes were reported on Sunday between seamen and truck drivers at the ports of Piraeus, Patras and Mytilini, police said.

The seamen's union has defied a court ruling on Friday that declared their strike illegal and vowed to press on with their action, campaigning for better pensions, insurance and favourable tax treatment.
"We will continue the strike and we feel quite calm about it," said John Halas, secretary general of the Panhellenic Seamen's Federation.
Civil aviation staff suspended work stoppages that crippled air transport in the past three days but threatened to resume their action if the government did not meet their economic demands.
High school teachers began an indefinite strike on Monday to press for better pay, while Greece's biggest labour confederation (GSEE) has announced a 24-hour nationwide walkout for Thursday.
GSEE is protesting against a new tax bill which abolishes a series of tax breaks for wage earners. The confederation also wants higher pensions for state pensioners and above-inflation pay rises.
The GSEE strike was expected to disrupt transport, state hospitals and public services. A number of state companies will be forces to operate with skeleton staff.
Technocrat Prime Minister Costas Simitis said his 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, was necessary bitter medicine for the country and has rejected all union demands.

He successfully stared down a crippling farmers' blockade that virtually cut the country in two in December, but farmers are threatening to block highways with their tractors again if demands for higher price supports, fuel and tax cuts are not met by February 4.
